subject: electronics
title: Sensor divider: darkness switches the lamp on

slides.heading: Sensor divider: darkness switches the lamp on
bullets: How a sensor divider switches a lamp on in the dark: as light falls the LDR resistance climbs, its share of the 6 V supply rises past the 4.5 V threshold
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we follow one sensor divider from bright daylight to darkness and watch the output climb until the lamp switches on.

slides.heading: What we will learn
bullets: Describe the sensor divider: a fixed resistor and an LDR in series across 6 V, with the output taken across the LDR
Explain why the voltage across the LDR rises from 1.2 V to 5.4 V as light falls, crossing the 4.5 V threshold only in the dark
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud and tell the class: by the end you will be able to trace the divided voltage at every light level and predict when the lamp lights.

slides.heading: A lamp that lights itself - how?
bullets: In bright daylight the lamp is off, with only 1.2 V across the LDR
So what changes as it gets dark - and why does the lamp switch on instead of off?
slides.notes: Ask the class: nobody touches a switch, yet the lamp lights at night - what must be changing inside the circuit? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because resistance decides the voltage share.

slides.heading: Shares in proportion to resistance
bullets: A potential divider splits the supply between series resistors in proportion to their resistances
Voltage across LDR = 6 V x R_LDR / (R_fixed + R_LDR), so the bigger resistance always takes the bigger share
An LDR's resistance rises as light falls, so its share - the output voltage - climbs in the dark
slides.notes: Stress the deciding idea: share follows resistance. The output is taken across the LDR, so when the LDR resistance grows, the output grows with it.

slides.heading: Bright daylight: the circuit assembles, lamp off
bullets: In bright daylight the LDR resistance is low, at 0.25 kOhm against the 1 kOhm fixed resistor
Its share is only 6 V x 0.25 / 1.25 = 1.2 V, far below the 4.5 V threshold, so the lamp stays off
slides.notes: Play scene 1 and point to the voltmeter: name the low LDR resistance and the small 1.2 V share it takes.

slides.heading: Light falls: resistance steps up, output climbs
bullets: As the light falls the LDR resistance steps up to 1 kOhm, equal to the fixed resistor
Equal resistances split the supply evenly, so the output climbs to 3.0 V - still below the threshold
slides.notes: Play scene 2 and watch the resistance step up: equal resistances mean equal shares, 3.0 V each.

slides.heading: Dusk: the output stops just below the threshold
bullets: At dusk the LDR resistance steps up again to 2.3 kOhm, more than twice the fixed resistor
Its share climbs to 4.2 V - close to, but still just below, the 4.5 V threshold, so the lamp stays off
slides.notes: Play scene 3 slowly: 4.2 V feels close, but close is not across - the lamp is still off.

slides.heading: Dark: the output crosses the threshold and the lamp lights
bullets: In the dark the LDR resistance rises to 9 kOhm, nine times the fixed resistor
It takes 5.4 V of the 6 V supply, crossing the 4.5 V threshold and switching the lamp on
slides.notes: Play scene 4 and follow the voltmeter past 4.5 V: the bigger resistance takes the bigger share, so darkness lights the lamp.

slides.heading: Worked example: reading the climb
bullets: At each stage use V = 6 V x R_LDR / (R_fixed + R_LDR): 1.2 V, then 3.0 V, then 4.2 V, then 5.4 V
Only the final 5.4 V beats the 4.5 V threshold, so the lamp lights only in the dark scene
slides.notes: Work it slowly: Step 1, bright daylight gives 1.2 V. Step 2, equal resistances give 3.0 V. Step 3, dusk gives 4.2 V, still short. Step 4, darkness gives 5.4 V and the lamp lights.

slides.heading: Your turn: predict the next stage
bullets: In pairs: if the LDR resistance rose to 19 kOhm, predict the output voltage and whether the lamp stays on
Then swap and check: did your partner use the share formula instead of guessing the voltage falls?
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes. Listen for share-formula reasoning, then take two pairs answers: 6 V x 19 / 20 = 5.7 V, above the threshold, so the lamp stays on.

slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
bullets: Your exit ticket asks you to correct a student who thinks the voltage across the LDR falls as it gets darker
Name the rising share and the 4.5 V threshold crossing to earn full credit
slides.notes: Point to the exit ticket and remind the class: the strongest answers trace the share rising with resistance until it crosses the threshold.
